## Campanha reforça a importância da identificação precoce de nódulos mamários; estudo brasileiro aponta que 70,2% das cadelas avaliadas com tumores mamários apresentavam sobrepeso ou obesidade

Quando o câncer é diagnosticado, o suporte nutricional passa a ter um papel importante - fotos FREEPIK

Quando o câncer é diagnosticado, o suporte nutricional passa a ter um papel importante fotos FREEPIK

Cristina Cruzcristina.cruz@odia.com.br

Publicado 11/10/2026 08:00

O Outubro Rosa, campanha de conscientização sobre o câncer de mama, também é um convite para ampliar os cuidados com a saúde dos animais de estimação. Em cadelas e gatas, os tumores mamários exigem atenção dos tutores, principalmente à identificação precoce de nódulos e outras alterações no corpo. Além do acompanhamento veterinário, a alimentação equilibrada e o controle do peso fazem parte dos cuidados com a saúde dos pets.
Um estudo brasileiro realizado pela Universidade Federal de Uberlândia (UFU) e publicado no Austral Journal of Veterinary Sciences analisou 600 cadelas diagnosticadas com tumores mamários. Entre elas, 54 apresentavam tumores benignos e 546, malignos. Os pesquisadores identificaram que 70,2% dos animais avaliados estavam com sobrepeso ou obesidade. O excesso de peso também foi associado a tumores de grau histológico II.

# Reclutamiento de bacterias para la terapia del cáncer

Las estrategias inmunoterapéuticas están diseñadas para estimular el sistema inmunitario a fin de combatir el cáncer. Dada la baja absorción de los fármacos inmunoterapéuticos por los tumores sólidos, los investigadores de CMI2T IA han empleado bacterias anaerobias para la administración de medicamentos en la zona del tumor.

 Salud  

Image © CMI2T IA

El cáncer constituye una de las principales causas de muerte en el mundo, lo que requiere el desarrollo de estrategias de tratamiento nuevas. La inmunoterapia se ha posicionado como un método robusto para estimular el sistema inmunitario a fin de combatir el cáncer y mantener una inmunidad duradera. Sin embargo, muy pocos agentes logran alcanzar y penetrar los tumores sólidos, lo que provoca a menudo efectos secundarios tóxicos relacionados con el sistema inmunitario. Además, algunos tumores desarrollan mecanismos de evasión y supresión inmunitaria, como la hipoxia tumoral, lo que limita aún más la absorción de los medicamentos. Bacterias modificadas genéticamente para la administración de medicamentos en los tumores El proyecto financiado con fondos europeos CMI2T IA se propuso administrar fármacos inmunoterapéuticos empleando bacterias anaerobias no patógenas.

# Una terapia experimental logra eliminar un tumor cerebral incurable en animales

Una investigación revela la eficacia de un nuevo tratamiento contra el glioblastoma, un tipo de cáncer muy agresivo. Se ha probado en modelos animales y consiste en la combinación de un fármaco y radioterapia focal cerebral.

Image: Ilustración de un tumor cerebral 

Ilustración de un tumor cerebral. / Universidad de Sevilla 

Image: SINC

 SINC 

  

Licencia Creative Commons 4.0

Un estudio revela una nueva terapia efectiva para el tratamiento contra el glioblastoma, un tipo de cáncer muy agresivo que se forma a partir de unas células llamadas astrocitos, que ayudan a que las neuronas funcionen correctamente. Este método terapéutico consiste en el uso concomitante del fármaco ADI-PEG20 –que elimina la arginina sistémica, lo que puede detener el crecimiento de las células cancerosas que necesitan de este aminoácido para crecer– junto con radioterapia cerebral focal.

Según el trabajo, llevado a cabo por investigadores del Instituto de Biomedicina de Sevilla (IBiS)y del Imperial College de Londres (Reino Unido), este doble tratamiento ha logrado eliminar por completo el tumor en los modelos animales usados en la investigación. Los resultados se publican en la revista The Journal of Clinical Investigation.

El doble tratamiento consiguió eliminar por completo el tumor cerebral en modelos in vivo, que fallecieron por causas naturales sin mostrar manifestación alguna de la enfermedad

En la actualidad, el glioblastoma es una enfermedad terminal cuya esperanza de vida media es menor a 2 años. Los tratamientos que se aplican hoy en día están basados en terapias de más de 30 años de antigüedad ya que, hasta la fecha, no se han producido avances significativos para combatir de forma eficiente este tipo de tumores.

Los resultados suponen una nueva propuesta terapéutica contra el glioblastoma: el uso del fármaco ADI-PEG20 en combinación con la aplicación de radioterapia focal cerebral. Con esto se logró observar cómo se conseguía eliminar por completo un tumor cerebral, incurable hasta la fecha, en modelos in vivo que fallecieron por causas naturales sin mostrar manifestación alguna de la enfermedad.

PharmaMar (MSE:PHM) ha anunciado hoy que el ensayo clínico fase III LAGOON, que evalúa Zepzelca® (lurbinectedina) para el tratamiento de pacientes con cáncer de pulmón de célula pequeña en segunda línea, ha alcanzado el objetivo de reclutamiento de 705 pacientes.

LAGOON es un ensayo clínico de fase III, aleatorio (1:1:1), multicéntrico y abierto, que consta de tres brazos: en el primer brazo, los pacientes reciben lurbinectedina en monoterapia; en el segundo brazo, se administra lurbinectedina en combinación con irinotecán; y en el tercer brazo, los pacientes son tratados con topotecán o irinotecán, según la elección de los investigadores. El objetivo principal del ensayo es evaluar la supervivencia global (OS, overall survival) y entre los objetivos secundario se evalúa la supervivencia libre de progresión (PFS, progression-free survival). Los primeros resultados del ensayo están previstos para el primer trimestre de 2026.

Lurbinectedina recibió la aprobación acelerada de la FDA en junio de 2020 para el tratamiento de pacientes adultos con cáncer de pulmón de célula pequeña metastásico con progresión de la enfermedad durante o después de una quimioterapia basada en platino. Desde entonces, ha sido aprobada en 17 territorios, incluido recientemente China, aunque en Europa únicamente ha recibido aprobación en Suiza.

# Clinical Trials for Dogs with Cancer

Links last verified: August 20, 2026

## Explore Current Research Trials in Canine Oncology

When a beloved dog is diagnosed with cancer, many families ask whether a clinical trial may provide an additional option. Canine oncology studies are conducted throughout the United States and around the world, but identifying an appropriate trial, and participating in one, can sometimes be challenging.

Each clinical trial has specific eligibility requirements.

These may include: 

  * A dog’s breed
  * Age
  * Weight
  * Overall health
  * Life expectancy
  * Cancer type
  * Cancer stage
  * Previous care
  * ...and other medical factors

Meeting a study’s general description does not guarantee acceptance. Pet parents should speak directly with the research team and their veterinary care provider to determine whether a trial may be appropriate for their dog.

It is also important to understand that clinical trials are not always free.

Research funding may cover only certain tests, medications, procedures, or appointments. Families may still be responsible for additional veterinary expenses, travel, lodging, and repeated visits over several weeks or months, especially when a study is located far from home.

The following links are intended to help pet parents and veterinary professionals find information about current canine oncology trials being conducted throughout the United States and, in some cases, internationally.

We encourage families to carefully review each study’s eligibility requirements, location, potential costs, time commitment, and possible benefits and risks with their veterinary team.

## Start Here: Nationwide Search Tools

If you are not sure where to begin, start with the AVMA registry. It lets you search by cancer type and by location, which is faster than checking individual centers one at a time.

#### AVMA Veterinary Clinical Trials Registry

The AVMA Veterinary Clinical Trials Registry, formerly known as the AVMA Animal Health Studies Database, helps dog parents and veterinary professionals find veterinary clinical studies taking place throughout the United States and Canada. By making this information easier to access, the registry supports continued research and progress in veterinary medicine and canine health care.

If you are interested in a clinical trial for your dog, begin by discussing the study and your dog’s potential eligibility with your veterinary care provider.

 

AVMA Clinical Trials

#### National Cancer Institute, Comparative Oncology Program

The Comparative Oncology Program develops and conducts clinical trials in partnership with veterinary teaching institutions throughout the United States. Dogs enrolled in these studies receive care from board-certified veterinary oncologists committed to improving comfort, quality of life, and cancer care for companion animals.

The knowledge gained through this research may help advance the understanding of cancer and support future progress in both canine and human oncology.

National Cancer Institute

#### PetCure Oncology

PetCure Oncology provides stereotactic radiation surgery and stereotactic radiation therapy, commonly known as SRS and SRT. These highly precise forms of radiation therapy have been used in human oncology and are now available for dogs with certain types of cancer.

PetCure Oncology reports using SRS and SRT in thousands of companion animals with a variety of tumor types. Its affiliated veterinary specialists continue to study these approaches to better understand their potential benefits, safety considerations, side effects, and appropriate applications in canine cancer care.

PetCure Oncology Clinical Trials

Network conducting trials at participating private practices.

## Keep in Mind

Clinical trials may explore new approaches to diagnosing or supporting dogs with cancer. These may include chemotherapy, radiation therapy, surgical procedures, temperature-based therapies, immunotherapy, photodynamic therapy, and other emerging approaches.

Although many clinical trials take place at veterinary colleges and teaching hospitals, a growing number of specialty and referral practices also participate in canine cancer research. Some studies require every appointment to be completed at the participating institution, while others may allow certain tests, procedures, or follow-up visits to be handled by a dog’s regular veterinary team.

The words “experimental” and “investigational” can understandably feel concerning. Before a new therapy or procedure reaches a veterinary clinical trial, researchers have typically completed earlier stages of evaluation. However, unknowns may remain regarding its safety, effectiveness, or potential side effects. A study is offered because researchers believe the approach may provide meaningful benefits, but participation does not guarantee a positive outcome.

Pet parents should review the study’s purpose, requirements, possible benefits, known and unknown risks, costs, and available alternatives with the clinical trial team and their dog’s veterinary care provider before making a decision.

# Comparative Oncology (Canine Trials and Resources)

Image: A physician and assistant examine a dog patient at the University of Minnesota

Credit: University of Minnesota

Enlarge Image

As in humans, cancers in pet dogs arise spontaneously. Dogs also have similar genomes, immune responses, living environment, and tumor complexity to humans. Studying pet dogs in cancer research, including in clinical trials, can provide valuable information for the development of future treatments for people.

The Integrated Canine Data Commons

The Integrated Canine Data Commons (ICDC) is a node in the larger NCI human Cancer Research Data Commons (CRDC). The Division of Cancer Treatment and Diagnosis (DCTD) developed the publicly available and searchable ICDC to incorporate genomic, proteomic, imaging, clinical trial, biomarker, population study, cancer model, and immuno-oncology data. This enables comparative analysis with tumors that arise spontaneously in pet dogs and advances research on human cancers.

PRECINCT Research Network: PRE-medical Cancer Immunotherapy Network Canine Trials 

In 2017, NCI granted five teams U01 awards (RFA-CA-17-001) and one team a U24 award (RFA-CA-17-002) to perform canine immunotherapy trials and correlative analyses. In 2022, the program was renewed with U01 awards (RFA-CA-21-050) issued to five new universities and a U24 award issued to the same team as in 2017 (RFA-CA-21-051). 
 
Learn more about the PRECINCT Network. 

Contact: Connie Sommers, PhD (sommersc@mail.nih.gov)

Immuno-oncology Canine Clinical Trials

DCTD is developing novel immuno-oncology agents for use in clinical trials involving pet dogs with cancer to inform, optimize, and better understand the underlying biology and administration of these agents in human patients. These canine-specific reagents target promising immune regulatory proteins. They will be useful not only as therapeutics, both as monotherapies and in combination with other cancer treatments, but also for pharmacodynamic assays and as imaging agents.

This multi-year, multi-phase, coordinated project is a collaboration between DCTD and the NCI Center for Cancer Research Comparative Oncology Program (COP). It leverages the COP’s veterinary clinical trial infrastructure (Comparative Oncology Trials Consortium) to advance the DCTD canine drug development pipeline. Newly developed agents will ultimately be shared with the extramural comparative oncology community to further cancer research.

Longitudinal Studies in Dogs with Cancer

The purpose of these studies is to obtain longitudinal tumor specimens that can be analyzed to inform our understanding of the molecular basis of canine cancer progression. In addition, this work will help determine whether pet dogs are a reliable model for evaluating the effectiveness of investigational therapeutics and treatment regimens for potential future use in humans.

Goals

  * Expand molecular studies to understand treatment and resistance throughout the development and evolution of malignant disease using pet dogs as a model

Objectives

  * To longitudinally track individual dogs that may receive treatments and/or participate in clinical trials or receive no treatment at the request of the owner (to study the natural history of the cancer in molecular detail)
  * To collect annotated canine cancer patient clinical/trial history and molecular characterization of biopsy material and blood at time of diagnosis, post-treatment, and at relapse. These will be used to to determine whether and in what circumstances naturally occurring tumors arise in dogs. They are good models of human cancer, tumor response, development of resistance to therapeutic regimens, and disease progression

Title: Pathology foundation models for training-free case retrieval in salivary gland tumors
Authors: Maximilian J. Roesel, Niklas Kiermeyer, Philipp Keyl, Frederick Klauschen

In pathology, pattern recognition relies on a frame of reference built through extensive training and experience, which may still fall short when encountering rare cancer subtypes. Archives of previously diagnosed tumors often contain relevant precedents, yet identifying the most relevant cases remains challenging. Here we explore whether content-based retrieval with current pathology foundation models facilitates rare cancer diagnostics without any task-specific training. Pathologists can query a digitized archive using a region of interest (ROI) from a whole slide image (WSI) and retrieve morphologically similar cases, along with their ICD-O codes and corresponding WSIs. The ROI can be selected manually or automatically using a gated attention-based multiple instance learning model. We evaluate our approach by leave-one-case-out on an imbalanced dataset of 137 salivary gland tumor cases spanning 12 ICD-O morphology categories, comparing four pathology foundation models (Atlas2, Atlas2-B, Atlas2-S, and UNI2h). Top-1/3/5 retrieval was 62.5%/76.7%/81.3% for Atlas2, 50.2/66.6/72.9% for UNI2h, 52.3%/71.5%/77.6% for Atlas2-B and 54.4/65.2/73.7% for Atlas2-S. Macro-averaged F1 ranged from 69.0% for the smallest model Atlas2-S to 76.6% for the largest model Atlas2 across the five classes with at least ten cases. Our modified Chamfer similarity separated correct from incorrect matches among the Top-5 more reliably for Atlas2 (AUC 0.754) than for Atlas2-B (0.679, p = 0.020) and Atlas2-S (0.653, p = 0.003), but not UNI2h (0.697, p = 0.196). Requiring no additional training or manual annotation, this approach makes departmental archives searchable with pathology foundation models, providing a low-barrier route to case-based differential diagnosis and extending the individual frame of reference to the collective experience of the department.

Purpose : To develop and evaluate CAPTOR, a deep-learning vision-language foundation model for oncologic chest-abdomen-pelvis (CAP) CT interpretation. Materials & Methods : CAPTOR (Chest-Abdomen-Pelvis foundaTion model for Oncologic Radiology) is a contrastive vision-language model, trained using a pretraining strategy for oncologic CAP CT (in single- or multiple-series acquisitions), on a multicenter retrospective dataset from North America, Europe and Asia, predominantly from tumor lesion examinations. CAPTOR was compared with state-of-the-art CT foundation models on three downstream tasks: disease detection, survival prediction using TumorImagingBench and image retrieval. Classification and retrieval were both evaluated on held-out internal and public test sets, stratified by anatomical coverage and indication.

Title: From Adults to Children: Benchmarking Foundation Models for Chest X-Ray Classification under Domain Shift
Authors: Sara Inácio, Hugo Proença, João C. Neves
Date: Thu Oct 15 12:57:08 2026

Foundation models have shown significant potential across diverse fields and have been applied to medical imaging, but their robustness across patient populations remains unclear. In this work, we investigate foundation models' ability to generalize from adult to pediatric chest X-ray classification. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first benchmark to compare multiple foundation models under a common adult-to-pediatric evaluation setting while also analyzing the effect of adaptation depth. We harmonize VinDr-CXR and PediCXR into a five-label classification task and evaluate six foundation models and two CNN baselines. All models are adapted using adult data only and tested in both the in-domain and pediatric domains using linear probing, partial fine-tuning, and full fine-tuning. The benchmark reveals a clear and consistent trend: all models suffer a substantial performance degradation when transferred from adult to pediatric data, with drops exceeding 10 percentage points. While Macro-AUROC values reach approximately 92% on the adult test set, performance decreases to around 78% on the pediatric domain. Another important finding is that increasing the depth of adaptation does not significantly improve cross-population generalization. Moreover, strong in-domain performance does not translate into better performance on pediatric data.
